candidate.answerReason: Nine purchases can give three of each color. Avoiding four of any color permits at most nine purchases, so the tenth guarantees four of one color.

methods.label: Find the largest purchase without four of a color
methods.explanation:
To avoid getting four gumballs of one color, a person can receive at most three of each color. With three colors, that allows at most
\[
3\times3=9
\]
gumballs.

Nine purchases really can fail to give four of a color: they could produce three red, three white, and three blue gumballs. The machine has enough of every color for this to happen.

A tenth gumball must belong to one of the three colors, pushing that color's count to at least four. Therefore the least number required is \(\boxed{10}\), choice \(\text{C}\).
methods.levelReason: A three-category capacity count and a possible worst-case purchase are elementary AMC 8 reasoning.

candidate.annotationRationale: The sharp guarantee requires both a universal capacity bound and an allowed nine-gumball example, fitting the extremal target. Multiplication as repeated addition supports the capacity calculation. The catalog's basic pigeonhole node guarantees only a repeated pair, so it is not assigned as the quantitative target for four of a color.

review.mathematicalCheck: Avoiding four of any color permits at most 3+3+3=9 gumballs. Three of each color is possible with the stated inventory, so nine can fail and ten guarantees the required four.
